evidence.title: 2025 El Teniente mining accident (encyclopaedia entry, read for the dated facts of the event itself)
evidence.excerpt: 31 July 2025 at 17:34 local: a magnitude 4.2 seismic event located 37 km north-east of Rancagua caused a collapse inside the Andesita sector of Codelco's El Teniente division, Machali. Six workers died, nine were injured. The last body was recovered on 2 August; national mourning was declared on 3 August. The collapse is described as a rock burst, not a construction failure.

evidence.title: Reuters: Codelco must send reports to restart underground mining after El Teniente collapse, government says
evidence.excerpt: Sernageomin imposed a formal suspension of underground operations at El Teniente and instructed Codelco to present four reports before it would evaluate lifting the measure: an analysis of the collapse's cause, a recovery plan, an assessment of the fortification systems in place, and a wider structural evaluation. The collapse damaged some 3.7 km of interior tunnels.

evidence.title: Reuters via US News: Codelco asks to restart part of El Teniente mine after accident
evidence.excerpt: Codelco suspended mining at El Teniente, the world's biggest underground copper mine, on the evening of Thursday 31 July, and six days later asked the regulator for permission to restart part of it. The mine produced more than 300,000 tonnes last year.

evidence.title: UPI: Chile's El Teniente copper mine resumes operations after fatal collapse
evidence.excerpt: On Saturday 9 August the El Teniente underground mine received approval from Sernageomin and the Labour Directorate to restart eight of its twelve underground sectors. Recursos Norte and Andesita remain suspended indefinitely after severe structural damage, to reopen only after engineering evaluation and remedial work.

evidence.title: Reuters via Mining.com: Codelco to lower 2025 copper target after El Teniente accident
evidence.excerpt: Codelco now expects 2025 production of 1.34-1.37 million tonnes, trimmed by 30,000 tonnes at both ends from its March guidance of 1.37-1.40 million. El Teniente is put at 316,000 tonnes for the year; the accident cost about 33,000 tonnes of output, some $340 million. Sectors in the expansion plan need to be revised. Half of El Teniente's twelve sectors have reopened.

evidence.title: World Socialist Web Site: Tunnel collapse kills 6, leaves 9 injured at Chile's El Teniente copper mine
evidence.excerpt: Names the contractors of the dead: Paulo Marin Tapia, an electrician, worked for Salfa Montajes; the five trapped miners (Gonzalo Nunez Caroca, Alex Araya Acevedo, Carlos Arancibia Valenzuela, Jean Miranda Ibaceta, Moises Pavez Armijo) worked for Gardilcic. Reports that Codelco had received the regulator's approval to reopen part of the mine.

evidence.title: Business and Human Rights Resource Centre: Constructora Gardilcic did not respond about the collapse at El Teniente
evidence.excerpt: The centre invited Constructora Gardilcic, the subcontractor employing five of the six dead, to respond to the collapse; the company did not. A parallel entry records Codelco's own response. The contractors directly involved had their contracts suspended by Codelco until at least 13 August.

evidence.title: Engineering and Mining Journal: Tragedy at El Teniente
evidence.excerpt: The trade press frames the event as a rock burst in the Andesita project area triggered by a magnitude 4.2 seismic event, with the question for investigators being whether the seismicity was induced by mining or tectonic. No account frames it as a tunnelling or construction defect in the first week.

evidence.title: Mining.com: Codelco collapse was likely caused by mining rather than nature (later technical finding, outside every call window)
evidence.excerpt: Later analysis concludes the seismic event was most likely induced by mining rather than natural tectonics. Recorded here because it revises the mechanism behind the narrative call without falling inside its five-day window: the framing at the time was seismicity, and the framing a year later is mining-induced seismicity.

evidence.title: COMEX copper daily closes, 25 July to 12 August 2025 (read through the harness price carrier)
evidence.excerpt: 31 July 2025: 4.3305, down 22.25% on the day after the US tariff proclamation exempted refined copper. Then 1 Aug 4.4125 (+1.89%), 4 Aug 4.4150 (+0.06%), 5 Aug 4.3640 (-1.16%). The largest close in the three sessions after the event is 1.96% above the 31 July level. The week's copper story is the tariff, not El Teniente.

evidence.title: Northern Miner: Codelco's El Teniente setback deepens copper fears (August 2026, the event this round was misdated onto)
evidence.excerpt: In August 2026 Codelco suspended development of the Andes Norte section at El Teniente for as long as two years after six months of analysis identified a seismic phenomenon associated with the depth of the project. Andes Norte is adjacent to Andesita and Teniente 7, where the July 2025 rockburst killed six workers. This is the 2026 El Teniente event; it is not a collapse.

resolutions.scorer_note: Branch whole_mine, not sector_only. Sernageomin imposed a formal suspension of the whole underground operation on the evening of 31 July; Codelco asked to restart part of it on 6 August; eight of twelve sectors were approved to restart on 9 August, with Andesita and Recursos Norte suspended indefinitely. Nine days whole-mine, against a falsifier set at seven. The second limb held exactly: the stated loss was 33,000 tonnes, tens of thousands, not hundreds. The baseline (a fatal underground failure stops the whole mine) had it, and had it for the right reason: the instrument the regulator reaches for is a suspension of the operation, not of a sector.

The narrative row is due first and is scored first. Every account in the first five days frames it as a rock burst in the Andesita sector triggered by a magnitude 4.2 seismic event, with the open question being whether the seismicity was induced by mining or tectonic. No account in that window frames it as a tunnelling or construction defect. The baseline (a tunnel collapse reported without a mechanism) missed: the mechanism was named on day one. Recorded against it: a year later the technical finding is that the seismicity was probably mining-induced, which revises the mechanism but falls far outside the window.

Codelco suspended mining at El Teniente on the evening of Thursday 31 July, publicly, within hours rather than the three days called. The seeded base rate (17 of 20 that a fatal underground collapse stops the affected sector) was the right denominator and the call did not need to depart from it. The stop was wider than the call said, which is the map call's miss, not this one's: this call asked whether the operator would stop the affected sector and say so.

Sernageomin acted at the site within a day: a formal suspension plus four required reports (cause, recovery plan, fortification assessment, structural evaluation) before it would evaluate lifting the measure, and it was the regulator, not the operator, that authorised the partial restart on 9 August. The call's declared departure from the seeded 4-in-20 rate was correct, because that rate counts orders reaching beyond the site and this is an order at it. The base rate was cited and departed from knowingly, which is what F3 asks.

No order suspending or inspecting underground mines beyond El Teniente inside thirty days appears in any carrier read. Coverage is thin and the call is scored accordingly: the only claim of a wider special-inspection programme comes from a content aggregator, unsupported by the regulator's own notices or by any wire, and an absence read off silence in English-language sources is worth less than the same absence read off the regulator's register. The base rate (4 of 20) pointed the right way.

The falsifier did not fire, and it is the falsifier that decides. ANTO closed 1877.0 on 31 July, 5.89% below the prior close and outside its own 20-session band of 3.33%, then 1890.0 (+0.69%) and 1922.5 (+1.72%) inside the band on 1 and 4 August. The out-of-band day cannot be the event: London closed at 15:30 UTC and the collapse was at 21:34 UTC, six hours later. What moved copper equities that day was the US tariff proclamation of 30 July, which took COMEX copper down 22.25% on 31 July. No carrier attributes any ANTO move to El Teniente in the window. This is the case the corrected band was built to expose: a band that can register an ordinary move now registers one, and only attribution keeps it from being counted as a re-encode.

The first limb is false: ANTO did close outside its own band on the event day (-5.89% against 3.33%), while FCX (+2.81% against 5.73%) and SCCO (+4.00% against 4.32%) stayed inside theirs. The ranking limb held, ANTO first and by a distance, but it held for a reason the call did not name: the London close is a tariff close, not a Chilean-supply close. Scored a miss because the claim as written said none would move, and scored mechanism unknown rather than right because a correct ordering produced by the wrong cause is not evidence for the ordering rule. The baseline (the largest producer by market value moves most) also missed.

Epiroc closed inside its 4.73% band on all five sessions from 31 July (-1.94%, -1.70%, 0.00%, +0.20%, -0.36%), and so did Sandvik on the same days. No carrier attributes anything at either name to the stoppage. The equipment order book is two classes away from a regulator's suspension notice and did not move on this timescale, which is what the call said and what the visibility ratio predicts for a single sector's development spend inside a global order book.

The absence failed on the tenth day. Salfa Montajes, a SalfaCorp subsidiary carried in the names book as an alias, is named in English-language coverage on 10 August as the employer of one of the six dead, alongside Gardilcic for the other five; the Business and Human Rights Resource Centre wrote to Gardilcic in the same window and recorded that Codelco had suspended the contractors' contracts until at least 13 August. The baseline (the contractor at a fatal site is named early) had it. The mechanism is scored wrong: the visibility ratio was cited to argue the fact would not reach the contractor's name, and the fact reached the name in ten days. What it did not reach is the price: SalfaCorp closed 717 on 31 July and 771 on 8 August, up 7.5% with the market, and its two out-of-band days in that window are 1.9% and 2.7% moves against a 1.47% band, which is noise on a thin listing rather than a re-encode. Named in the press, unpriced in the equity: the class gap held even though the naming test failed.

Copper closed 4.3305 on 31 July and 4.4125, 4.4150 and 4.3640 over the three sessions after: the highest is 1.96% above the event-day level, under the 3% called, and no carrier in the window attributes a copper move to El Teniente. Stated confound, and it is a large one: the copper price that week was doing something else entirely, falling 22.25% on 31 July on the US tariff proclamation, so the call was right about the size of the tonnage but was scored against a week in which the benchmark was not free to answer the question.

On 21 August, twenty-one days in and well inside the forty-five called, Codelco cut 2025 guidance to 1.34-1.37 million tonnes from 1.37-1.40 million and put El Teniente at 316,000 tonnes, naming 33,000 tonnes and about $340 million of lost output. The call carried a no-base-rate reason rather than a rate, and the reason was the right one: a state-owned producer with bond-market disclosure duties speaks on output, and there is still no denominator in the store for how fast.
